Burst traffic handling and autoscaling policies

summary: QuantaPay evaluated Redwood Dedicated for a low-latency fraud/risk assistant workload with strict p95 latency SLOs and bursty traffic (payday/weekend spikes). Redwood demo covered Dedicated GPU pools, routing, and Console observability. QuantaPay focused on how Redwood keeps p95 predictable under burst, what happens when capacity is exhausted (queueing vs 429), and how fallback policies work without surprising output changes. Redwood proposed a POC with traffic replay and an agreed benchmarking window, and to share a Dedicated sizing recommendation (GPU type + replicas) along with suggested autoscaling/burst configuration and rollout guardrails.

transcript:
Meeting: QuantaPay + Redwood Inference — Dedicated capacity demo / latency & burst Q&A
Recorded by Fireflies.ai
Date: Thu, May 8, 2025 10:02 AM PT
Duration: 47 min

Attendees
- Priyom Das (Redwood, AE)
- Markus Klein (Redwood, Solutions Engineering)
- Maya Patel (QuantaPay, Eng Manager)
- Daniel Cho (QuantaPay, Staff Infra)
- Elena Ruiz (QuantaPay, PM)
- Tom Becker (QuantaPay, Security/GRC)


Summary (auto-generated)
QuantaPay asked detailed questions on predictable latency under burst traffic, how Redwood Dedicated handles capacity limits, and what operational controls exist (rate limits, queues, fallback). Redwood demoed Console dashboards and explained rollouts and model version pinning.

Topics (auto-generated)
1) Dedicated capacity basics
2) Console: latency / cost / errors
3) Burst behavior and autoscaling
4) Rollouts + fallback policies
5) Security / isolation (high level)

Action items (auto-generated)
- Redwood to send sizing + POC plan
- QuantaPay to provide traffic distributions


Transcript
[00:00] Priyom Das: Cool, thanks everyone for joining. I’m Priyom, I work with the QuantaPay team on the commercial side. Markus is here, he’ll do most of the technical demo.

[00:12] Markus Klein: Hey all. Thanks for the time. I’m going to share screen. If at any point you want to interrupt, please do.

[00:23] Maya Patel: Sounds good.

[00:26] Markus Klein: Alright. Quick agenda: I’ll do like ten minutes on what “Dedicated” means in Redwood terms, then Console dashboards, then we can go deep on latency predictability and burst handling, because I know that’s the big concern.

[00:44] Elena Ruiz: Yep, that’s the main thing.

[00:47] Markus Klein: Cool. So Dedicated: you’re reserving a GPU pool that is isolated for your org. Requests for your API key route only to that pool. It’s not like the hosted shared fleet where you’re sharing capacity. We can configure min replicas, max replicas, and burst behavior depending on the contract.

[01:07] Daniel Cho: When you say isolated, do you mean like single tenant nodes, or just like quotas?

[01:12] Markus Klein: Single-tenant GPU workers. Like, at the node level you’re not co-tenanted with other customers’ inference processes. We still run our control plane, but the data plane is dedicated for you.

[01:25] Tom Becker: And logs and such—like request logs—where do those live? Just high level.

[01:31] Markus Klein: High level: Console gives you telemetry. We do not store prompt/response bodies by default in Dedicated. We store operational metadata like latency, token counts, error codes. Audit logs for admin actions—like API key creation, model changes—those are available. We can go deeper in a security review, but for today I’ll keep it scoped.

[01:55] Priyom Das: Yeah and we can loop Naomi from our security team if needed after.

[02:00] Maya Patel: Okay.

[02:02] Markus Klein: Let me show the Console. So this is a demo tenant. Left nav: Routes, Models, Deployments, Observability. Under Observability you get latency by route, model, region. You can slice p50, p90, p95.

[02:22] Markus Klein: Here—this chart is p50 and p95 over time. And then token-level breakdown: time to first token, decode time, queue time.

[02:32] Elena Ruiz: Queue time is key for us. Because our current setup, when it’s busy, queue goes crazy.

[02:38] Markus Klein: Exactly. And the reason we show it explicitly is it helps answer “is the model slow” vs “is the system saturated.” In Dedicated, you can decide what happens under saturation.

[02:52] Daniel Cho: Like what are the options? Do you queue, do you reject, do you shed load?

[02:56] Markus Klein: All three. Typically it’s: keep a small bounded queue, and after a threshold return 429 with Retry-After. For certain use cases we also do a “soft failover” to a fallback model if you’ve configured it.

[03:12] Maya Patel: Wait, fallback model—do you mean like to a smaller model?

[03:15] Markus Klein: Usually, yes. Like same family but cheaper/faster, or a quantized profile. But it’s policy-driven. You can turn it off completely if output consistency is more important than uptime.

[03:30] Priyom Das: And the fallback is something we’d set up together with you in the POC, not just like magic.

[03:37] Elena Ruiz: We have a fraud analyst assistant workflow. If we suddenly swap models, we might change decisioning. So we’d probably rather fail than silently change.

[03:48] Markus Klein: That’s a common stance. What we do is: you can configure fallback to be only for specific routes, like your lower-risk “draft explanation” route, not the “final recommendation” route.

[04:04] Daniel Cho: Okay. Can you show error breakdowns? Like timeouts vs rate limits.

[04:08] Markus Klein: Yep. Errors tab—this is grouped by status code and by root cause. You’ll see 5xx, 429, timeouts. And we add “capacity exhausted” vs “upstream model error” etc.

[04:22] Daniel Cho: Do you export metrics? Prometheus or something.

[04:26] Markus Klein: For Dedicated we can push to your system via OTEL export, and we also have webhooks for certain events. Again, depends on how you want to run it.

[04:37] Maya Patel: What about the model deployment piece. Like we’d want to test a new version without breaking p95.

[04:44] Markus Klein: That’s rollouts. In Deployments you’ll see “model version pinning.” So you don’t get surprise changes. When we onboard a new engine or new quant, you opt in. Then canary: route 5% of traffic to v2, compare latency and quality metrics, and then roll forward.

[05:06] Elena Ruiz: Can you A/B test? Like route by header.

[05:09] Markus Klein: Yes. Header-based routing and also by cohort key. Some folks do “user_id mod 100” style.

[05:18] Priyom Das: And for the case where you want strict control, you can just keep the version fixed until you explicitly approve.

[05:26] Daniel Cho: The big question: predictable latency. Our internal SLO is p95 under 350ms for a particular route, not including network. We see bursty traffic—paydays, weekends, random spikes. How does Dedicated help and what do you guarantee?

[05:45] Markus Klein: Great. So first, Dedicated helps because you’re not contending with other customers. Second, we do capacity planning around your tokens per second requirement, not just requests per second. For generation workloads, tokens out is the big driver.

[06:05] Markus Klein: In the Console you can see tokens/s, and we can set alerts when you’re approaching saturation. If you have a burst, there are a few knobs: (1) pre-warm additional replicas, (2) allow burst capacity—like extra GPUs that can come online, (3) use batching strategically.

[06:26] Daniel Cho: Batching increases latency though.

[06:28] Markus Klein: It can, yes. We use continuous batching, and we aim to keep time-to-first-token stable. For some workloads, you can batch more on embeddings and keep generation less batched. But you’re right, there’s a trade.

[06:45] Maya Patel: We care about time to first token because it’s in a UI.

[06:49] Markus Klein: Right. We separate TTFT and total completion time. For interactive, you cap batching and you ensure decode is prioritized.

[07:00] Elena Ruiz: We also have an async pipeline for some of it. But the high priority one is interactive.

[07:06] Priyom Das: Maybe it helps if you share: what’s the peak? Like is it 2x or 10x.

[07:12] Daniel Cho: It’s… depends. Our “steady” is like 50 RPS on that route, but spikes can be 200, 250 RPS for short windows. Tokens out average maybe 120? But long tail goes to like 600.

[07:30] Markus Klein: Got it. That tail matters. For sizing we’d use percentiles: input tokens p50/p95, output tokens p50/p95. Then we can calculate tokens per second.

[07:43] Daniel Cho: What happens if we exceed? Do you queue? Or do you just start slowing down.

[07:48] Markus Klein: If you exceed sustained capacity, you’ll see queue time go up. We recommend a bounded queue and then rejecting beyond. Otherwise your p95 gets destroyed and it cascades.

[08:01] Maya Patel: So you’ll 429 us.

[08:03] Markus Klein: If configured, yes, with a Retry-After. Or we can do per-route rate limits. The point is to keep your “good” requests good.

[08:13] Elena Ruiz: We’ve been burned by autoscaling that takes minutes, so by the time it scales, the spike is over.

[08:19] Markus Klein: Yep. GPU scale-up isn’t instant. So we try to plan: for known spikes, you schedule scale ahead. For unknown, you keep headroom. There’s also burst pools, but those have constraints.

[08:34] Priyom Das: On the contract side we can talk about reserved + burst capacity options. We usually start with reserved and then add burst if the traffic is truly spiky.

[08:45] Daniel Cho: When you say burst pool, is it still dedicated? Or do we share.

[08:49] Markus Klein: Burst can be dedicated to your account but not always sitting warm. Think of it as extra capacity that can be allocated, but there’s a warm-up time. Some customers accept that for best-effort overflow. If you need “no warm-up,” you keep it reserved.

[09:10] Maya Patel: So predictable latency equals keeping enough reserved GPU to cover your peak.

[09:14] Markus Klein: Exactly, for the strict SLO route. Another approach is to have two tiers: SLO-critical on Dedicated reserved, non-critical on Hosted or on a cheaper route.

[09:28] Elena Ruiz: We probably keep everything in Dedicated if possible, because the compliance team is touchy.

[09:34] Tom Becker: It’s more about isolation and control. If it’s shared, we have more questions.

[09:39] Priyom Das: Understood.

[09:41] Markus Klein: Let me show rollout + fallback in practice. Here’s a deployment with “primary model” and “compatible variants.” If the primary is saturated, you can choose: (A) reject, (B) queue, (C) fail over.

[09:58] Elena Ruiz: Compatible variants… is that like same model but quantized.

[10:02] Markus Klein: Often yes. For example, same architecture but 8-bit quant. Or a smaller model. We can label it as “fallback” and you can restrict it by route.

[10:13] Daniel Cho: How do you ensure output doesn’t change too much.

[10:16] Markus Klein: You run evals. We have an eval harness where you can run a prompt set across models/versions. Then you compare metrics and do human review. It’s not perfect but it’s the right control.

[10:31] Maya Patel: Do you provide that or do we.

[10:33] Markus Klein: We provide tooling and integration points. Many customers bring their own golden set.

[10:41] Priyom Das: And for the POC we can define acceptance criteria not just latency, but also quality checks.

[10:49] Elena Ruiz: Okay.

[10:51] Daniel Cho: Let’s get specific. If we have 250 RPS spike, and you sized for 200, do we get a cliff? Like everything 429? Or partial.

[11:00] Markus Klein: You can do per-route prioritization. So your high priority route gets capacity reserved, lower priority routes get rate limited first. So it’s not a total cliff.

[11:12] Daniel Cho: That’s important. Today we have no prioritization, it’s just a big queue.

[11:16] Markus Klein: Exactly. It’s essentially QoS.

[11:20] Maya Patel: And how do you define priority.

[11:23] Markus Klein: Route-based. Also headers. Like “x-priority: high.”

[11:30] Elena Ruiz: That’s feasible.

[11:33] Tom Becker: Quick security question: do you support customer-managed keys. Like KMS.

[11:38] Markus Klein: In Dedicated, yes, we can integrate with cloud KMS for encryption at rest, and we can do key ownership models depending on deployment. For Private it’s fully customer-owned. For Dedicated it’s integrated with your KMS.

[11:55] Tom Becker: Okay, we’ll follow up offline.

[11:58] Markus Klein: Back to burst. Another thing is KV cache reuse. If your prompts have a common prefix, we can cache that. Sometimes it reduces GPU time meaningfully.

[12:10] Daniel Cho: KV cache… sorry, key value cash.

[12:12] Markus Klein: (laughs) Key-value cache, yes. Prefix caching.

[12:16] Maya Patel: We do have common system prompts.

[12:18] Markus Klein: That’s usually a quick win. It helps with latency and cost.

[12:24] Elena Ruiz: We also do function calling sometimes. Like structured outputs.

[12:28] Markus Klein: Yep. We support tool calling and JSON schema style structured output, and we track parse success rate.

[12:39] Daniel Cho: Another question: what about region. We need us-east.

[12:43] Priyom Das: We can do Dedicated in us-east, yes. We’ll confirm exact AZ options once we scope.

[12:51] Maya Patel: And data retention. We don’t want prompts stored.

[12:55] Markus Klein: Correct. Not stored by default. We keep metrics. If you enable logging for debugging, it’s opt-in and time bounded.

[13:05] Elena Ruiz: Okay.

[13:08] Markus Klein: Let’s pivot to measurement. For predictable latency, we recommend a benchmarking plan. You replay representative traffic at different loads, measure p50/p95/timeout rate, and confirm behavior at saturation.

[13:25] Daniel Cho: We can do traffic replay. We have k6 scripts and a gateway.

[13:29] Markus Klein: Perfect. We’ll align on the measurement window, like 30 minutes at steady, 10 minutes spike, include warm cache and cold cache.

[13:41] Maya Patel: I want to know how you define p95. We had vendors where they exclude errors, or they drop slow requests.

[13:47] Markus Klein: Good question. In Console, p95 is computed over successful responses by default, but you can include errors and see separate distributions. We’ll define it in the POC doc so it’s apples-to-apples.

[14:03] Priyom Das: Yeah we’ll put it in writing. We’ve learned this the hard way too.

[14:07] Elena Ruiz: Great.

[14:09] Daniel Cho: What about streaming. Do you support streaming. And does it change p95.

[14:14] Markus Klein: We support streaming. We measure TTFT and then stream stability metrics. For p95, if you’re streaming, TTFT is usually the SLO, not total completion.

[14:28] Maya Patel: For UI, yes, TTFT.

[14:31] Markus Klein: Exactly.

[14:33] Elena Ruiz: Can we cap output tokens. Because the tail is huge.

[14:37] Markus Klein: Yes, max_tokens per request and also per-route caps. And you can enforce it so you don’t have one request hogging decode.

[14:47] Daniel Cho: That helps with predictability.

[14:50] Markus Klein: It does.

[14:52] Priyom Das: I’m watching time; we have like ~30 minutes left but I think we hit the key areas. Do you want to see anything else in Console. Like cost dashboards.

[15:02] Elena Ruiz: Yes, cost per request would be helpful.

[15:05] Markus Klein: Okay. Cost tab: you can see cost per 1K tokens, total tokens in/out, and per-route. In Dedicated, pricing is usually capacity-based, but the cost view still helps for internal chargeback and identifying heavy routes.

[15:24] Maya Patel: So even if we pay a flat monthly, it helps us allocate internally.

[15:28] Markus Klein: Exactly.

[15:31] Daniel Cho: Do you show GPU utilization.

[15:34] Markus Klein: We show a proxy: tokens/sec and queue time, and we can share deeper utilization via export. Some customers don’t want raw infra metrics in the UI, but we can provide.

[15:49] Tom Becker: Competitors question. We’re also looking at Bedrock and possibly OpenAI direct. Their story is “we’ll handle scaling.” But we keep seeing noisy neighbor issues. So Dedicated is attractive. But how do you compare.

[16:04] Priyom Das: Totally fair. Bedrock/OpenAI are great for speed. Where Dedicated wins is: predictable performance for your specific workload, control over rollouts and versioning, and single-tenant isolation. Also, we can do open model choices if needed.

[16:22] Markus Klein: And specifically on burst: on shared APIs you don’t control what happens at the fleet level. You can get rate limited without warning. With Dedicated, you define your own policies.

[16:35] Daniel Cho: Yeah, that’s the crux.

[16:38] Elena Ruiz: What’s the typical lead time to spin up Dedicated.

[16:42] Priyom Das: Once we scope, it’s usually days not weeks, depending on region and the exact GPU type. We’ll give you a concrete timeline after we get your traffic info.

[16:55] Maya Patel: Okay.

[16:57] Markus Klein: One more thing: rollbacks. If you do a canary and p95 regresses, we can automatically rollback. You define thresholds.

[17:08] Daniel Cho: Like p95 > X.

[17:10] Markus Klein: Exactly. Or error rate > Y.

[17:14] Maya Patel: That’s helpful. We had a regression last month and it took hours to identify.

[17:21] Markus Klein: Yep.

[17:24] Priyom Das: Maybe we should talk POC. I know you have a scoping call penciled next week?

[17:29] Maya Patel: We haven’t scheduled, but yes, we want to.

[17:33] Priyom Das: Great. We’ll send times.

[17:36] Daniel Cho: For POC, we want: hit our p95 TTFT under 350ms, maintain error rate under 0.5%, handle a 5x spike for 5 minutes without falling over. And we want deterministic behavior when you exceed capacity.

[17:55] Markus Klein: Love it. We’ll turn those into measurable acceptance criteria. Also define the exact prompts and token limits.

[18:05] Elena Ruiz: And we should include quality. Like at least “no worse than baseline.”

[18:10] Markus Klein: Agreed.

[18:12] Tom Becker: And security review in parallel.

[18:15] Priyom Das: Yep. We can run that alongside.

[18:18] Markus Klein: Anything else you want to see in the UI.

[18:21] Maya Patel: No, I think this is good.

[18:23] Daniel Cho: Can you send a write-up on the burst options. Like reserved vs burst pool.

[18:28] Priyom Das: Yes.

[18:29] Markus Klein: I’ll also send a sizing worksheet request. Basically we need your input/output token percentiles.

[18:37] Daniel Cho: Okay.

[18:39] Priyom Das: Great. Let’s do a quick recap so we’re aligned.

[18:43] Priyom Das: Recap: Dedicated gives you single-tenant capacity, predictable latency based on sizing, policies for queue vs 429, route prioritization, and controlled rollouts with canary and rollback. Next we’ll do a POC scoping call. Daniel you’ll share traffic stats. Tom you’ll share the security questionnaire. Markus will send sizing recs and a short note on burst.

[19:07] Maya Patel: Sounds right.

[19:09] Elena Ruiz: Yep.

[19:10] Daniel Cho: Yep.

[19:12] Tom Becker: Works.

[19:14] Priyom Das: Cool, thanks everyone.

[19:16] Markus Klein: Thanks.

[19:18] (call ends)
